clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant, adult-onset (typically fifth to sixth decade), slowly progressive pure cerebellar syndrome that is among the more benign spinocerebellar ataxias
Caused by a small CAG repeat expansion in CACNA1A, which encodes the alpha-1A subunit of the P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel
Downbeat and gaze-evoked nystagmus and other cerebellar oculomotor signs are characteristic and often early
Some patients experience episodic ataxia or migraine, reflecting the allelic overlap of CACNA1A with episodic ataxia type 2 and familial hemiplegic migraine
Extracerebellar features (marked spasticity, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive decline) are usually mild or absent compared with other polyglutamine SCAs
MRI shows relatively isolated cerebellar (especially vermian) atrophy with a comparatively preserved brainstem
Anticipation is limited because the expanded repeat is small and relatively stable across generations
Management is supportive, centred on physiotherapy, gait and balance rehabilitation, and treatment of any coexisting migraine or vertigo
reference.pathophysiology: SCA6 results from a modest expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat within CACNA1A, the gene encoding the pore-forming alpha-1A subunit of the P/Q-type (Cav2.1) voltage-gated calcium channel that is densely expressed in cerebellar Purkinje cells. The expanded polyglutamine tract alters channel function and promotes intracellular accumulation of the mutant subunit, leading to selective, slowly progressive degeneration of Purkinje cells and the cerebellar cortex. Because CACNA1A also harbours point mutations causing episodic ataxia type 2 and familial hemiplegic migraine, SCA6 sits within an allelic spectrum of channelopathies, which explains overlapping episodic and migrainous features in some patients.
additionalDifferentials: Other autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxias, particularly SCA1, SCA2 and SCA3
additionalInvestigations: Targeted CACNA1A CAG repeat-expansion analysis to confirm the diagnosis
MRI brain demonstrating predominantly cerebellar atrophy with relative brainstem sparing
Broader ataxia repeat-expansion panel when the initial test is negative
Nerve conduction studies to assess for coexisting neuropathy and help distinguish from other SCAs
Vestibular and oculomotor testing to characterise nystagmus and imbalance
Exclusion of acquired causes with vitamin, thyroid, autoimmune and paraneoplastic screening
redFlags: Abrupt or stepwise deterioration suggesting a superimposed vascular or structural lesion rather than SCA6 alone
Prominent autonomic failure raising suspicion of multiple system atrophy
Rapid progression or subacute onset pointing to an acquired (paraneoplastic or immune) cause
Recurrent disabling episodic ataxia or migraine warranting reassessment for an episodic-ataxia phenotype
reference.prognosis: SCA6 is typically the most slowly progressive of the common polyglutamine ataxias, with many patients remaining ambulant for years and life expectancy often near normal. Disability accrues gradually through worsening gait ataxia, dysarthria and oculomotor dysfunction.
pitfalls: Attributing a slowly progressive late-onset ataxia to ageing or alcohol and omitting genetic testing
Overlooking coexisting episodic ataxia or migraine that is treatable in its own right
Assuming marked anticipation and unnecessarily alarming families, given the repeat's relative stability
Confusing the isolated cerebellar atrophy of SCA6 with the olivopontocerebellar pattern of multiple system atrophy
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
